title: Ἄνθρωπος καὶ λέων ⟨συνοδεύοντες⟩
titleEn: The Man and the Lion Travelling Together
part: The Man and the Lion Travelling Together (Chambry 59 · Perry 284)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 59 (= Perry 284). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A lion was once travelling with a man.
sentences.n: Chambry supplies ⟨συνοδεύοντες⟩, 'travelling together', in the title inside angle brackets: the editor's words, added to the manuscript heading, not the manuscripts' own.

sentences.t: Ἕκαστος δὲ αὐτῶν τοῖς λόγοις ἐκαυχῶντο.
sentences.tr: Hekastos de autōn tois logois ekauchōnto.
sentences.l: And each of them were boasting with their words.
sentences.i: And each of them boasted as they talked.
sentences.n: ἕκαστος is singular but ἐκαυχῶντο is plural — the sense ('each of the two') pulls the verb into the plural, which Greek allows freely. τοῖς λόγοις is a dative of means, 'by their talk'.

sentences.t: Καὶ δὴ ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ ἦν ἀνδρὸς στήλη πετρίνη λέοντα πνίγοντος.
sentences.tr: Kai dē en tēi hodōi ēn andros stēlē petrinē leonta pnigontos.
sentences.l: And indeed on the road there was a stone monument of a man throttling a lion.
sentences.n: πνίγοντος agrees with ἀνδρός across the words between: 'of a man … throttling a lion'. A στήλη is an upright carved slab. The fable does not name the figure, but a man throttling a lion is the standard image of Heracles and the Nemean lion.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἀνὴρ ὑποδείξας τῷ λέοντι ἔφη· « Ὁρᾷς σὺ πῶς ἐσμεν ὑμῶν κρείττονες. »
sentences.tr: Ho de anēr hypodeixas tōi leonti ephē· « Horāis sy pōs esmen hymōn kreittones. »
sentences.l: And the man, having pointed it out to the lion, said: « You see how we are stronger than you. »
sentences.n: Chambry prints a full stop, not a question mark, so the words read as much as a taunt as a question. ὑμῶν is a genitive of comparison after κρείττονες — 'stronger than you', plural because it is man against lion as kinds, not two travellers.

sentences.t: Κἀκεῖνος εἶπεν ὑπομειδιάσας· « Εἰ λέοντες ᾔδεισαν γλύφειν, πολλοὺς ἂν ἄνδρας εἶδες ὑποκάτω λέοντος. »
sentences.tr: Kakeinos eipen hypomeidiasas· « Ei leontes ēideisan glyphein, pollous an andras eides hypokatō leontos. »
sentences.l: And he, having smiled faintly, said: « If lions knew how to carve, you would have seen many men beneath a lion. »
sentences.n: A contrary-to-fact condition: εἰ with ᾔδεισαν (pluperfect in form, imperfect in sense, 'knew') in the protasis, ἄν with the aorist εἶδες in the apodosis — what would be so, but is not. Κἀκεῖνος is καὶ ἐκεῖνος run together by crasis. The whole joke turns on who holds the chisel.

sentences.t: Ὅτι πολλοὶ καυχῶνται διὰ λόγων ἀνδρεῖοι εἶναι καὶ θρασεῖς οὓς ἡ πεῖρα γυμνασθέντας ἐξελέγχει.
sentences.tr: Hoti polloi kauchōntai dia logōn andreioi einai kai thraseis hous hē peira gymnasthentas exelenchei.
sentences.l: That many boast through words to be brave and bold, whom experience, once they have been exercised, convicts.
sentences.i: The story shows that many boast in words that they are brave and daring, but experience puts them to the test and shows them up.
sentences.n: A bare Ὅτι moral: the 'the story shows' is unexpressed in the Greek, which opens simply 'That…', and is supplied in the idiomatic line. καυχῶνται … εἶναι is an infinitive after a verb of claiming; γυμνασθέντας agrees with οὓς, 'them, once they have been exercised'. ἐξελέγχω is to cross-examine a man until the truth comes out — a courtroom word.
